Plotting plasma glucose levels vs. age shows that the two response groups, 
`Non-diabetic` and `Diabetic`, show a substantial overlap. 
`Diabetes` would therefore not be easily predicted by `Age` and `Glucose`
in a standard logistic regression model which would not be able to derive 
a straight line clearly separating the groups.

## Logistic regression model 

The vector form of the probailistic equation for a logistic regression model is
$$
P(Y = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{sigmoid}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{T}\mathbf{x})
$$ {#eq-logistic}
where the sigmoid function is
$$
\operatorname{sigmoid}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{T}\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{T}\mathbf{x}}}
$${#eq-sigmoid}

For `Diabetes` as the binary target/response (y), and `Glucose` and `Age` as features/predictors (x1, x2):

$$
P(Y = 1 \mid x_1, x_2) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\theta_0 + \theta_1 x_1 + \theta_2 x_2)}}
$${#eq-logistic-expanded}
Training a logistic regression model on the (entire) provided data set, using glm() in R, results in the following probabilistic equation

$$
P(Y=1 \mid x_1,x_2) =
\frac{1}{1 + e^{-(
`r round(logistic_coef1["(Intercept)"], 4)` +
`r round(logistic_coef1["Glucose"], 4)`x_1 +
`r round(logistic_coef1["Age"], 4)`x_2)}}
$${#eq-logistic-fitted}

The training misclassification error for this model is `r round(training_misclass_error, 2)`.

## Decision boundary equation

Setting the probabilistic equation @eq-logistic-fitted = r (here = 0.5) 
 gives the decision boundary equation as
$$
`r round(logistic_coef1["(Intercept)"], 4)` +
`r round(logistic_coef1["Glucose"], 4)`x_1 +
`r round(logistic_coef1["Age"], 4)`x_2 = 0
$$
Solving this for `Glucose` gives the (approximate) linear decision boundary line:

$$
Glucose = - `r round(logistic_coef1["(Intercept)"]/logistic_coef1["Glucose"],2) - `r round(logistic_coef1["(Intercept)"]/logistic_coef1["Glucose"],2)`
$$
